evidence: M-O s.v. bon appétit: libenter cēnā (cēnāte, comede, comedite)
Cic. Fin. 2.24: quī bene cēnent omnīs libenter cēnāre
Cato Agr. 156.1: sī volēs in convīviō multum bibere cēnāreque libenter
terms.comment: The wish is modern (Egger, as Morgan–Owens gives it), made of a classical phrase: libenter cēnāre is to enjoy one’s dinner, in Cato and in Cicero, who says that all who dine well dine with pleasure, but not all who dine with pleasure dine well. At other meals, libenter prande, libenter jentā; to several, libenter cēnāte.

terms.gloss: do eat, please (the host’s invitation to begin)

evidence: M-O s.v. bon appétit: bene tibi (vōbīs) sapiat
terms.comment: A modern wish; bene sapit, it tastes good, is said of the food (see “yum yum”).

phrases.latin: ex quō illud efficitur, quī bene cēnent omnīs libenter cēnāre, quī libenter, nōn continuō bene.
phrases.english: from which it follows that all who dine well dine with pleasure, but those who dine with pleasure do not necessarily dine well.

phrases.latin: itaque et ēdit et bibit … et jūcundē, opiparē sānē et apparātē nec id sōlum sed bene coctō et condītō, sermōne bonō et, sī quaeris, libenter.
phrases.english: and so he ate and drank … and with pleasure, lavishly indeed and in style, and not only that, but food well cooked and seasoned, with good talk, and, if you want to know, he enjoyed it.

sources: Lewis & Short: libet · Lewis & Short: ceno · Lewis & Short: vescor · Lewis & Short: sapio
